fine_tuned_food101_test_set.method: torchvision Food101 official test split (manually verified, not the noisier train split); top1/top3 computed by model-training/kaggle/train_kaggle.py's evaluate() after each epoch, reported for the final/best epoch (15)

imagenet_linear_probe_baseline.method: ImageNet-pretrained efficientnet_lite0 with the backbone frozen (requires_grad=False on every non-classifier parameter, whole model held in eval() mode so BatchNorm running stats stay put); only a fresh 101-class linear head trained, on the Food-101 train split; evaluated on the same official test split as the fine-tuned run. Ran on Kaggle GPU via model-training/kaggle/baseline/baseline_kaggle.py.
imagenet_linear_probe_baseline.why_a_linear_probe: A pretrained backbone carries a 1000-class ImageNet head, so Food-101 accuracy isn't directly computable for it without deciding what stands in for the head. A linear probe isolates the question that matters: how separable are the frozen ImageNet features on Food-101, and therefore what did unfreezing the backbone actually buy?

untrained_head_reference.method: Epoch 0 of the same baseline run: frozen backbone, fresh 101-class head, zero training. Recorded to show why this is NOT used as the headline baseline — it measures chance (1/101 = 0.0099), so '85.78% vs 1.08%' would be a true but empty comparison.

finetuning_gain_over_linear_probe.method: fine_tuned_food101_test_set minus imagenet_linear_probe_baseline, same test split, same architecture. This is the measured answer to 'did fine-tuning the backbone help, and by how much.'
